themes.theme: Conformity assessment before market entry or use, and re-assessment on change
themes.definition: The formal check that a high-risk AI system meets the AI Act's requirements before it is placed on the market or put into service, who carries it out (the provider itself, a notified body, a market surveillance authority or the AI Office), and when it must be repeated.
themes.what_is_set_out: The AI Act requires every high-risk system to undergo a conformity assessment before it is placed on the market or put into service (Art. 16(f), Recital 123) and makes the provider responsible for making sure it happens. For the Annex III use cases in points 2 to 8, which the coder note says cover most public-sector uses such as essential public services and law enforcement [inference], the provider follows internal control (Annex VI), a self-assessment that 'does not provide for the involvement of a notified body'; Recital 125 calls self-assessment the general rule 'with the only exception' of biometrics, where Annex VII lets a notified body examine the quality management system and technical documentation and run its own tests if not satisfied with the provider's. Two routes are specific to the public sector: where a high-risk system is to be put into service by law enforcement, immigration or asylum authorities or by EU institutions, the market surveillance authority acts as the notified body (Art. 43(1)), and the Omnibus makes the AI Office responsible for conformity assessments and tests of certain systems subject to third-party assessment (Art. 75(1e)). A new assessment is required on a substantial modification even if the system 'continues to be used by the current deployer' (Art. 43(4)) and when the intended purpose changes (Recital 128); certificates last at most five years for Annex I and four years for Annex III systems. Importers, distributors and authorised representatives check paperwork (CE marking, declaration of conformity, documentation) rather than the system. The Omnibus adds that systems meeting the Cyber Resilience Act are deemed to meet the Art. 15 cybersecurity requirements, lets notified bodies under product legislation assess AI conformity, and allows product manufacturers to avoid third-party assessment only if harmonised standards covering all Section 2 requirements were applied; notified bodies must be independent of the provider (Art. 31(4)).
themes.holders: Providers of high-risk AI systems (self-assessment and duty to ensure assessment); notified bodies; the market surveillance authority acting as notified body for law enforcement, immigration, asylum and EU-institution systems; the AI Office (Omnibus); importers, distributors and authorised representatives (paper checks); product manufacturers under Annex I legislation.
themes.binding: Statutory duties ('shall') in the AI Act and the Omnibus, with recitals ('should') as non-binding explanation. Breach of the provider's duty to ensure conformity assessment (Art. 16(f)) is recorded by the coders as fineable up to EUR 15 000 000 or 3% of worldwide turnover under Art. 99(4)(a); importers and distributors face parallel fines under Art. 99(4)(c) and (d). The passages state no further consequence of a failed assessment beyond the absence of a certificate.
themes.checks: Trigger: before placing on the market or putting into service; again on substantial modification, change of intended purpose, or expiry of a certificate (maximum five years Annex I, four years Annex III). Compared against: the requirements of Chapter III Section 2 (Arts 8-15) and, for the quality management system, Art. 17; harmonised standards or common specifications where applied. Metric or threshold: not stated. Who: the provider alone for Annex III points 2-8; a notified body for biometrics where standards were not fully applied; the market surveillance authority for law enforcement, immigration, asylum and EU-institution systems; the AI Office for systems under Art. 75(1). Result: declaration of conformity and, for notified bodies, a reasoned assessment decision and certificate; a notified body not satisfied with the provider's tests may carry out its own.

quotes.quote: providers shall follow the conformity assessment procedure based on internal control as referred to in Annex VI, which does not provide for the involvement of a notified body
the market surveillance authority referred to in Article 74(8) or (9), as applicable, shall act as a notified body
Where the notified body is not satisfied with the tests carried out by the provider, the notified body shall itself directly carry out adequate tests, as appropriate.

quotes.location: Art. 1(31)(c), inserting AI Act Art. 75(1e); p. 27
quotes.quote: The AI Office shall be responsible for conformity assessments and tests of AI systems referred to in paragraph 1 of this Article that are classified as high-risk and subject to a third-party conformity assessment pursuant to Article 43

themes.theme: Provider risk-management system across the lifecycle
themes.definition: The continuous process by which the provider of a high-risk system identifies, evaluates and reduces risks to health, safety and fundamental rights until the remaining risk is judged acceptable.
themes.what_is_set_out: Article 9 requires a risk management system to be 'established, implemented, documented and maintained' for every high-risk system, run as a continuous iterative process over the whole lifecycle, with risks removed or reduced first through design and the residual risk of each hazard and of the system 'judged to be acceptable' (Art. 9(5)). Providers must consider whether the system is likely to harm people under 18 and other vulnerable groups (Art. 9(9)). The recitals add that providers should document and explain the measures they choose, 'when relevant, involve experts and external stakeholders', and measure themselves against 'the generally acknowledged state of the art' (Recitals 64-65). The Commission's guidelines on prohibited practices present this risk management, together with the other high-risk requirements, as a way of keeping a high-risk system from becoming a prohibited practice. None of the passages says who judges residual risk acceptable or against what threshold.
themes.holders: Providers of high-risk AI systems; Art. 9 itself is in the passive voice and the coders identify the provider through Arts 9(9) and 16(a).
themes.binding: Statutory duty (Art. 9) explained by non-binding recitals. The coders record that breach of Art. 16(a) (compliance with Section 2) is fineable up to EUR 15 000 000 or 3% under Art. 99(4)(a), outside these passages. The acceptance criterion has no named decision-maker.
themes.checks: Trigger: continuous over the lifecycle, with regular systematic review. Compared against: known and reasonably foreseeable risks to health, safety and fundamental rights under intended use and reasonably foreseeable misuse; the state of the art. Metric or threshold: residual risk 'judged to be acceptable'; who judges and against what threshold is not stated. Who: the provider. Result: mitigation measures, documented choices, and input to testing (Art. 9(8)) and technical documentation.

quotes.quote: A risk management system shall be established, implemented, documented and maintained in relation to high-risk AI systems.
the relevant residual risk associated with each hazard, as well as the overall residual risk of the high-risk AI systems is judged to be acceptable

providers shall give consideration to whether in view of its intended purpose the high-risk AI system is likely to have an adverse impact on persons under the age of 18 and, as appropriate, other vulnerable groups
t he risk assessment and management done by the provider and the compliance with the other requirements for high-risk AI systems (e.g., data governance, transparency and human oversight)

themes.theme: Risk classification and assessment of each AI system by the institution using it
themes.definition: Requirements, mostly in EU institutions' own frameworks and in guidance to public administrations, that the body using AI classify each system by risk and assess and mitigate its risks before and during use.
themes.what_is_set_out: Several EU institutions set themselves a per-system risk assessment. The Commission will 'classify and assess AI systems in use – or planned to be used' with a risk-based approach and its operational guidelines; its IT and Cybersecurity Board checks at project initiation that ethical, legal and regulatory compliance is taken into account, a register of systems in use is 'assessed against corporate guidelines and legal requirements', and internal generative AI tools are assessed case by case under corporate IT governance. The European Parliament says validation processes should include a risk assessment and an impact assessment covering risks such as transparency and cybersecurity and organisational impact, completed 'as an integral part of every AI project', with assessment frameworks reviewed regularly, regular assessment of long-term safety and risks in its roadmap, and control and assurance mechanisms to be developed by its ICT services. The Court of Auditors commits to assess each use case against the AI Act's risk categories, to assess AI components in HR processes for risk, transparency and human-in-the-loop controls, and to apply enhanced safeguards for HR, administrative services and auditee data. EDPS guidance tells EUIs to analyse 'each AI system they plan to use' for likelihood and impact, to devise mitigation for each lifecycle phase, to compare operational results against identified risks, and to run a generative-AI risk assessment, while stressing that guidance does not replace the controller's own compliance assessment. JRC129100 frames the same idea as recommendations to public administrations: identify where risks are likely to be highest, apply context-specific mitigation, and complement checklists with assessment tools.
themes.holders: The European Commission (internal AI governance, the IT and Cybersecurity Board, the ISG-AI and corporate governance boards); the European Parliament's administration and ICT services (often unnamed); the European Court of Auditors; EUIs as data controllers (EDPS); public administrations (JRC). Several passages name no assessor.
themes.binding: Internal institutional requirements and commitments ('will', 'shall' within internal frameworks, 'should'); EDPS restates the statutory accountability duty of EUIs under the EUDPR but frames the method as guidance; JRC is recommendation. Only EP2024 attaches a consequence: non-compliance with the assessment process 'should lead to the suspension of the AI project'.
themes.checks: Trigger: before use (planned systems, project initiation, before budget is committed), then regularly or on change; the Commission register is continuous. Compared against: risk-based classification and internal operational guidelines (Commission); AI Act risk categories (ECA); risk types such as transparency and cybersecurity and organisational impact (EP); the organisation's own risk criteria and the identified risks (EDPS). Metric or threshold: qualitative likelihood and impact in EDPS (a five-level scale per the coder note); otherwise not stated. Who: Commission boards and AI governance; EP services; the ECA; the controller. Result: mitigation measures and register entries; in the Parliament, possible suspension of the project.

quotes.quote: Classify and assess AI systems in use – or planned to be used by the Commission – based on a risk-based approach and using the Commission’s operational guidelines.

quotes.location: page 4, III. Risk and impact assessment processes…
quotes.quote: Such assessments should be completed as an integral part of every AI project.
EUIs should perform a thorough analysis for each AI system they plan to use in order to also evaluate the likelihood and impact of the risks
assessing each use case against the Act’s risk categories, implementing the required transparency and oversight measures, and maintaining documentation to demonstrate conformity.

themes.theme: Quality and representativeness of training, testing and input data
themes.definition: Requirements to govern, check and maintain the data used to train, validate and test AI systems, and the input data fed to them in use, so that it is relevant, representative, accurate and free of errors.
themes.what_is_set_out: The AI Act requires training, validation and testing data sets for high-risk systems to be subject to data governance practices and to be 'relevant, sufficiently representative, and to the best extent possible, free of errors and complete' for the intended purpose (Art. 10), including an examination for possible biases; the Omnibus restates this as 'quality criteria'. A deployer that controls input data must ensure it is relevant and sufficiently representative (Art. 26(4)), one of the few data duties that falls on public bodies as users. EDPS guidance turns this into procedures for EUIs: sample the training dataset and measure it 'against the agreed quality threshold' set in a quality-assurance policy, run regular data-quality and bias audits, detect and correct outliers, compare the statistical distribution of training and intended input data, verify data against reliable sources and through review by domain experts, and validate the relevance of planned data types before full training; procured systems should be checked for how close training demographics are to the people the system will process. EDPS's generative AI orientations add curation, labelling, periodic review and use of trusted sources, including for third-party data. The Parliament's 2020 guidelines say only 'Use representative datasets' and that training samples 'should cover all possible corner cases', and its 2024 framework points to data-governance rules still being developed; the Court of Auditors and JRC state data quality as a general need for public institutions, and EU090 advises GPAI providers to remove illegal content from training data.
themes.holders: Providers of high-risk systems (Art. 10 is passive; the coders name the provider); deployers that control input data (Art. 26(4)); EUIs and controllers (EDPS); subject-matter experts (EDPS); Parliament's administration (implied); public institutions (ECA); GPAI providers (EU090). Many EDPS measures name no holder.
themes.binding: Statutory in the AI Act and Omnibus, with breach of Art. 16(a) or Art. 26 recorded as fineable under Art. 99(4); 'to the best extent possible' softens Art. 10(3). EDPS measures are 'possible measures' or 'should'; EP2020 uses imperatives with no consequence; ECA and JRC are statements of principle; EU090 is advisory.
themes.checks: Trigger: during development (training, validation, testing) and before full training; regular audits; deployer checks during use. Compared against: the intended purpose and the persons or groups on whom the system is used (AI Act); an agreed quality threshold in the organisation's own policy (EDPS); the population in which the system will be used and the distribution of intended input data. Metric or threshold: none set in the AI Act; EDPS refers to the organisation's own threshold and to statistical comparison (histograms, summary statistics per coder notes). Who: the provider; the deployer for input data; controllers or domain experts in EUIs. Result: correction or removal of data, rebalancing; otherwise not stated.

quotes.quote: Training, validation and testing data sets shall be relevant, sufficiently representative, and to the best extent possible, free of errors and complete in view of the intended purpose.
that deployer shall ensure that input data is relevant and sufficiently representative in view of the intended purpose of the high-risk AI system
Define and implement a procedure for assessing the training personal dataset which, in accordance with the policy, samples the dataset, measures and assess es against the agreed quality threshold.

quotes.location: page 5, Ethical and Lawful Artificial Intelligenc…
quotes.quote: Use representative datasets to train and test the AI model.

themes.theme: Testing and validation against defined metrics before and during deployment
themes.definition: Testing of a system's performance, robustness and fitness for purpose against metrics, test data, adversarial examples or end-user needs, before deployment and when it changes.
themes.what_is_set_out: The AI Act's core rule is that testing of high-risk systems 'shall be carried out against prior defined metrics and probabilistic thresholds' appropriate to the intended purpose, during development and in any event before market entry (Art. 9(8)); the quality management system must set test and validation procedures and their frequency, and Annex IV requires the metrics, their appropriateness and test results to be documented. The provider chooses the metrics and thresholds; the Act sets none. GPAI models with systemic risk must be evaluated with 'standardised protocols and tools reflecting the state of the art', including documented adversarial testing. EDPS guidance describes verification and validation that checks 'statistical accuracy, r obustness, and generalisability using test and validation datasets' against requirements set at inception, testing on diverse data and edge cases, separate validation and test sets, measures against overfitting, red teaming, and tests that retrieval-augmented systems do not leak personal data; it also suggests buyers request evaluation metrics from providers. The EU institutions' own frameworks are thinner: the Parliament requires use cases to be 'identified, tested and validated' with end users, folds risk and impact assessment into validation, and asks whether performance tests will uncover data problems and whether the right algorithm is used; the Court of Auditors is the only document to touch prompts, proposing 'appropriate quality controls and documentation' for its translation prompt library, and stresses the ability to validate and audit algorithms. JRC calls for collecting practice to identify validation tools, and the EDPB treats the controller's tests of a model against known attacks as evidence about anonymity.
themes.holders: Providers of high-risk systems; notified bodies (own tests); providers of GPAI models with systemic risk; developers (EDPS GenAI); EUIs and controllers (EDPS, EDPB); the Parliament's administration (often unnamed); the ECA Language and Editorial Directorate; public institutions (ECA).
themes.binding: Statutory for providers under the AI Act (fines via Art. 16(a) and Art. 99(4)(a)) and for GPAI providers (Art. 55, fines under Art. 101 per coder notes); EDPS and EDPB are guidance or interpretation ('should', 'possible measure'); EP2024 'must' within an internal framework; EP2020 poses questions; the ECA prompt-library item is an option ('could explore').
themes.checks: Trigger: during development and before placing on the market or deployment; at final evaluation; on retraining (the new version is validated); for the Parliament, before use [inference]. Compared against: prior defined metrics and probabilistic thresholds appropriate to the intended purpose (AI Act); functional and non-functional requirements set at inception (EDPS); state-of-the-art protocols (GPAI); real-world scenarios and edge cases; end-user needs (EP); the organisation's objectives for procured systems. Metric or threshold: categories are named (accuracy, robustness, statistical accuracy, generalisability, discriminatory impact) but no values; values are left to the provider or the organisation. Who: the provider, developer or controller; for the Parliament, not stated. Result: recorded in technical documentation and test reports; otherwise not stated.

quotes.quote: Testing shall be carried out against prior defined metrics and probabilistic thresholds that are appropriate to the intended purpose of the high-risk AI system.

quotes.location: p.10, s.3.2 Lifecycle of an AI system (phase 4)
quotes.quote: to ensure it meets the functional and non -functional requirements set in the inception stage. This involves checking the AI system's statistical accuracy, r obustness, and generalisability using test and validation datasets
Relevant use cases must be identified, tested and validated through an inclusive process, involving the end-users.
further developing the directorate’s prompt library, with appropriate quality controls and documentation.

themes.theme: Accuracy, robustness and security of AI systems
themes.definition: Requirements that AI systems reach and keep an appropriate level of accuracy, resilience to errors and attacks, and security of the model and its data.
themes.what_is_set_out: Article 15 requires high-risk systems to 'achieve an appropriate level of accuracy, robustness, and cybersecurity' and to 'perform consistently in those respects throughout their lifecycle', to limit biased feedback loops in systems that keep learning 'as far as possible', and to resist data poisoning, adversarial examples and other attacks; the accuracy level is not quantified but is declared by the provider in the instructions for use, and Annex IV records accuracy for specific groups. The Omnibus deems systems meeting the Cyber Resilience Act compliant on cybersecurity. EDPS guidance translates security into AI-specific controls for EUIs: protect training, input and output data and the model itself, prevent outputs reproducing training data, secure APIs with multi-factor authentication, logging and penetration tests, and add controls for prompt injection, jailbreaks and model inversion with continuous monitoring of their effectiveness. Accuracy also appears in its data-protection sense, that personal data must not be 'incorrect or misleading as to any matter of fact', which EDPS separates from statistical accuracy; its generative AI orientations require controllers to 'ensure data accuracy at all stages' and say EUIs should reconsider use if accuracy cannot be maintained. For biometric identification, the prohibited-practices guidelines ask the FRIA to describe the system's performance and accuracy and suggest that national law may regulate 'the minimum reliability, threshold used, and accuracy rates', without values; for generative systems, informing users of limitations and building in safeguards against hallucination can keep false outputs outside the ban on deception. The Parliament, JRC143539 and the Court of Auditors state the aims in general terms, and the Parliament routes risks from AI tools it does not offer to its cyber-security framework.
themes.holders: Providers of high-risk systems and GPAI models (AI Act; Art. 15 is passive); EUIs and controllers (EDPS); law enforcement deployers and Member States via national law (EU043); providers of generative systems (EU043); Parliament's administration (implied); public administrations (JRC143539); the ECA.
themes.binding: Statutory in AI Act Art. 15 (fines via Art. 16(a)), qualified by 'appropriate', 'as far as possible' and 'where appropriate'; EDPS restates EUDPR security and accuracy duties but frames most measures as possible measures; EU043 is non-binding interpretation; EP, JRC and ECA are internal requirements or statements of principle.
themes.checks: Trigger: throughout the lifecycle (AI Act); verification, validation and ongoing operation (EDPS); regular security audits. Compared against: intended purpose and the state of the art; the provider's declared accuracy metrics; known attack types. Metric or threshold: 'appropriate level', not quantified; levels and metrics declared by the provider in the instructions for use (Art. 15(3), per coder note); EU043 names reliability, threshold and accuracy rates as possible content of national law without values. Who: the provider; the controller; Member State law for biometric identification. Result: not stated, except EDPS that EUIs should reconsider use if accuracy cannot be maintained.

quotes.quote: High-risk AI systems shall be designed and developed in such a way that they achieve an appropriate level of accuracy, robustness, and cybersecurity, and that they perform consistently in those respects throughout their lifecycle.
Data controllers must ensure data accuracy at all stages of the development and use of a generative AI system.
the minimum reliability, threshold used, and accuracy rates of the systems used;
Ensuring AI safety means putting in place controls that guarantee predictable, explainable, and reliable outcomes.

themes.theme: Bias and fairness checks on data, models and outputs
themes.definition: Requirements to examine, measure and correct biases and discriminatory outcomes in AI systems, their training data and their outputs, including the legal basis for processing sensitive data to do so.
themes.what_is_set_out: The AI Act requires training data for high-risk systems to be examined 'in view of possible biases' that may harm health, safety or fundamental rights or lead to prohibited discrimination, and continuously learning systems to limit biased feedback loops. The Omnibus creates a legal basis for providers, and for deployers of high-risk systems, to process special categories of personal data 'exceptionally' to detect and correct bias, with records of why this was strictly necessary, while stating that the deployer permission 'does not create any obligation' to carry out bias detection. EDPS guidance is the most concrete: controllers should 'identify and measure these biases', audit the algorithm's performance 'across different demographic groups' and assess disparities, test on diverse data, consider fairness-aware algorithms, audit how analysts interpret outputs, and ask providers for fairness metrics. EDPS's generative AI orientations tell EUIs to 'test and regularly monitor if the system output is biased' with their own input data rather than relying on providers, and to have mechanisms for continuous monitoring and correction. The Parliament's 2020 guidelines ask 'Are we avoiding bias in the algorithm?' and require 'control mechanisms to detect biases', without metrics; JRC143539 asks for design that promotes fairness and equal treatment; the prohibited-practices guidelines warn that a provider or deployer aware that its system discriminates and taking no corrective action may be treated as exploiting vulnerabilities.
themes.holders: Providers (AI Act Art. 10; Omnibus Art. 4a); deployers of high-risk systems (permission only); controllers and EUIs (EDPS); Parliament's administration (implied); providers and deployers aware of discrimination (EU043); public administrations (JRC143539).
themes.binding: Statutory for the provider's examination of data (Art. 10); permissive ('may') for processing sensitive data under the Omnibus, with mandatory conditions if used; EDPS measures are guidance; EP2020 is an internal checklist; EU043 is interpretation whose consequence is that the system may fall within a prohibition.
themes.checks: Trigger: during development (data examination); regular audits; ongoing monitoring of outputs; procurement (metrics requested from the provider). Compared against: performance across demographic groups; real-world scenarios; the deploying institution's own business data. Metric or threshold: EDPS names false positive rate parity, false negative rate parity and calibration fairness and recommends calculating several metrics (coder notes); no thresholds anywhere. Who: the provider; the controller; the EUI as deployer. Result: correction of data or model and records of special-category processing; otherwise not stated.

quotes.quote: examination in view of possible biases that are likely to affect the health and safety of persons, have a negative impact on fundamental rights or lead to discrimination prohibited under Union law
Conduct regular audits of the AI system to check for biases. This involves evaluating the algorithm's performance across different demographic groups and identifying and assessing any disparities.
EUIs know best their business case and should test and regularly monitor if the system output is biased by using input data tailored to their business needs.

quotes.location: Art. 1(6), inserting AI Act Art. 4a(2); p. 17
quotes.quote: Providers and deployers of other AI systems and models and deployers of high-risk AI systems may exceptionally process special categories of personal data to the extent that:

themes.theme: Technical documentation and recording of design, testing and decisions
themes.definition: Duties to draw up and keep up to date written records of how a system or model was designed, trained, tested and changed, and of assessments and decisions made about it.
themes.what_is_set_out: The AI Act requires technical documentation to be drawn up before a high-risk system is placed on the market and kept up to date (Art. 11), and Annex IV sets minimum contents that bear directly on output quality: what the system 'is designed to optimise for', 'the expected output and output quality', key design choices and assumptions about the people it is used on, any use of third-party pre-trained tools, the metrics for accuracy, robustness and discriminatory impact and why they are appropriate, accuracy for specific groups, the human oversight measures needed, and the post-market monitoring plan. A provider that decides an Annex III system is not high-risk must document that assessment before market entry (Art. 6(4)); each use of post-remote biometric identification must be documented in the police file and made available to the market surveillance and data protection authorities. GPAI providers keep model documentation including training, testing and evaluation results (Art. 53, Annex XI) for each model and throughout its lifecycle, and the Commission expects them to document assumptions and uncertainty in compute estimates. Data-protection texts add documentation duties for controllers: the EDPB reads GDPR record-keeping as covering AI training and lists test reports 'by whom, when, how and to which extent'; EDPS asks for documentation of datasets and models, data sources, pre-processing and modelling decisions, DPIA decisions across the lifecycle, and metadata to trace personal data. The Code of practice on marking and labelling requires signatories to document their compliance processes.
themes.holders: Providers of high-risk systems (Arts 11, 16, 18; Annex IV is passive); providers and downstream modifiers of GPAI models; deployers of post-remote biometric identification; prospective providers in sandboxes; controllers and EUIs (EDPB, EDPS); actors involved in a DPIA; signatories of the Code (EU121).
themes.binding: Statutory under the AI Act (fines via Art. 99(4); the coders note that under Art. 83(1)(g) the market surveillance authority acts if documentation 'is not available') and under GDPR/EUDPR as restated; Commission and EDPB interpretation; EDPS 'should'; Code commitments bind signatories only and are monitored by market surveillance authorities with no consequence stated.
themes.checks: n/a (a recording duty, not a check); but this is where the results of checks must be kept: metrics and test logs and reports (Annex IV points 2(g), 3, 4), the post-market monitoring plan (point 9), and test reports for AI models (EDPB para 58(e)).

quotes.quote: The technical documentation of a high-risk AI system shall be drawn up before that system is placed on the market or put into service and shall be kept up-to date.
what the system is designed to optimise for, and the relevance of the different parameters; the description of the expected output and output quality of the system
reports on how the model has been tested (by whom, when, how and to which extent) and (iv) the results of the tests
Datasets and models must be accompanied by documentation on their structure, maintenance and intended use.

themes.theme: Automatic logging and retention of logs
themes.definition: Requirements that AI systems automatically record events during use and that providers and deployers keep these logs for a minimum period.
themes.what_is_set_out: High-risk systems must 'technically allow for the automatic recording of events (logs) over the lifetime of the system' (Art. 12), so that events relevant to risks, substantial modifications and post-market monitoring can be traced. For remote biometric identification, minimum logs include the period of each use, the reference database, the input data that led to a match and 'the identification of the natural persons involved in the verification of the results', tying logging to human review. Providers (Art. 19) and deployers (Art. 26(6)) must keep logs under their control for at least six months, subject to data-protection law; deployers here include public bodies [inference]. The prohibited-practices guidelines restate the six-month rule for biometric identification and say logs should be made available to the authorising authority to show that an urgent request was timely. Sandbox processing logs must be kept for the duration of participation, and EDPS adds logging and monitoring of API calls as a security measure.
themes.holders: Providers (build the logging capability and keep logs under their control); deployers of high-risk systems; prospective providers in sandboxes; law enforcement deployers of biometric identification; EUIs (EDPS).
themes.binding: Statutory (AI Act Arts 12, 19, 26(6); fines via Art. 99(4) per coder notes); EU043 restates; EDPS lists logging as a possible measure.
themes.checks: Logging records rather than checks; it supports other checks. Trigger: continuous over the system's lifetime; for biometric identification, each use. Compared against: n/a. Metric or threshold: retention of at least six months. Who: the provider and the deployer. Result: logs available for post-market monitoring, investigations and authorities; otherwise not stated.

quotes.quote: High-risk AI systems shall technically allow for the automatic recording of events (logs) over the lifetime of the system.

shall keep the logs automatically generated by that high-risk AI system to the extent such logs are under their control, for a period appropriate to the intended purpose of the high-risk AI system, of at least six months
The logging of the processing activities should be made available to the authority to substantiate the timeliness of the request.
Implement logging and monitoring for API calls.

themes.theme: Post-market monitoring, incident investigation and corrective action by providers
themes.definition: The provider's duty to collect and analyse performance data after a system is on the market, to investigate serious incidents and risks, and to correct non-compliant systems.
themes.what_is_set_out: Providers of high-risk systems must establish and document a post-market monitoring system that 'actively and systematically' collects and analyses performance data, including data supplied by deployers, over the system's lifetime, based on a plan that forms part of the technical documentation (Art. 72; restated by the Omnibus); Recital 155 adds analysis of interaction with other AI systems where relevant. After a serious incident the provider must investigate, assess the risk and take corrective action (Art. 73(6)), and when it learns that a system presents a risk it must investigate the causes with the reporting deployer (Art. 20(2)). Operators must take corrective action across every system they have made available when an authority finds a problem (Arts 79(4), 82(2)), and a provider whose system is reclassified as high-risk must bring it into compliance (Art. 80(4)). The prohibited-practices guidelines say providers may monitor for compliance with use restrictions they impose, and GPAI providers with systemic risk must track and document serious incidents.
themes.holders: Providers of high-risk systems; operators; providers of GPAI models with systemic risk.
themes.binding: Statutory. Consequences named in the coder fields: market surveillance authorities can require corrective action, withdrawal or recall and take provisional measures (Art. 79(5)); a provider that fails to comply after reclassification is subject to fines (Art. 80(4)). The EU043 monitoring item is optional ('may').
themes.checks: Trigger: ongoing after placing on the market; on a serious incident; on a finding of risk, non-compliance or misclassification. Compared against: continuous compliance with the Chapter III Section 2 requirements (Art. 72(2), per coder note). Metric or threshold: not stated. Who: the provider, using data from deployers; the operator for corrective action. Result: investigation, risk assessment and corrective action within the authority's timeline; otherwise not stated.

quotes.quote: The post-market monitoring system shall actively and systematically collect, document and analyse relevant data which may be provided by deployers or which may be collected through other sources on the performance of high-risk AI systems throughout their lifetime

quotes.location: Art. 1(30), replacing AI Act Art. 72(3); p. 26
quotes.quote: The post-market monitoring system shall be based on a post-market monitoring plan. The post-market monitoring plan shall be part of the technical documentation referred to in Annex IV.
it shall immediately investigate the causes, in collaboration with the reporting deployer, where applicable

Where appropriate, such measures may also include monitoring for compliance with that restriction, depending on the means through which the AI system is supplied and the information at the provider’s disposal for possible misuse .

themes.theme: Deployer duties when using high-risk systems
themes.definition: What the AI Act requires of organisations, including public bodies, that use a high-risk system: use it as instructed, monitor it, check the input data and keep logs.
themes.what_is_set_out: Deployers must take technical and organisational measures to use high-risk systems 'in accordance with the instructions for use', monitor their operation on that basis and, where relevant, inform providers (Art. 26(1) and (5)), ensure that input data under their control is relevant and representative (Art. 26(4)), and keep the logs for at least six months (Art. 26(6)). The yardstick for the deployer's monitoring is the provider's instructions, not a standard the deployer sets. The prohibited-practices guidelines restate that deployers 'remain responsible for taking the lawful conditions for the use of the system into account', and present the deployer's duties of appropriate use, human oversight and, 'in some cases', a FRIA as means of avoiding prohibited practices.
themes.holders: Deployers of high-risk AI systems, which include public authorities [inference].
themes.binding: Statutory (Art. 26), recorded by the coders as fineable under Art. 99(4)(e); the recital and EU043 restate or interpret.
themes.checks: Trigger: ongoing during use. Compared against: the provider's instructions for use; the intended purpose (for input data). Metric or threshold: not stated. Who: the deployer. Result: inform the provider where relevant; otherwise not stated in these passages.

quotes.quote: Deployers of high-risk AI systems shall take appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure they use such systems in accordance with the instructions for use accompanying the systems
Deployers shall monitor the operation of the high-risk AI system on the basis of the instructions for use and, where relevant, inform providers in accordance with Article 72.
deployers remain responsible for taking the lawful conditions for the use of the system into account.

themes.theme: Ongoing monitoring of performance, drift, bias and outputs in operation
themes.definition: Checks during operation that a deployed system keeps working as expected, including performance tracking, drift detection, retraining, review of risk assessments and regular review of outputs.
themes.what_is_set_out: Beyond the AI Act's provider-centred post-market monitoring, guidance addressed to EU institutions describes what monitoring in use involves. EDPS's risk guidance says a deployed system 'needs continuous monitoring to ensure it operates as expected', with regular assessment against test data that may need updating, data drift detection, retraining 'on a fixed schedule (e.g. weekly or monthly) or triggered by performance drops or detected drift', and comparison of operational results with the identified risks; it calls for 'a culture of accountability, continuous monitoring and adaptive improvement'. EDPS's generative AI orientations require 'regular monitoring' of output data and inferences 'including human oversight', regular checks for bias with the institution's own data, monitoring that no personal data is processed where not intended, and regular review of risk assessments because the model 'may exacerbate identified risks or create new ones'. The prohibited-practices guidelines say continuous compliance 'necessitates ongoing monitoring of and updates to' systems; the Parliament's 2020 guidelines call for 'control mechanisms to detect biases and unintended consequences' and a 'continuous verification process'; JRC129100 calls for monitoring supported by feedback from citizens, businesses and public administration operators. None names a metric value or a responsible role within the using institution beyond 'controllers' or 'EUIs'.
themes.holders: EUIs and data controllers (EDPS); providers and deployers (EU043); Parliament's administration (implied); not stated in several passages, including most EDPS lifecycle passages.
themes.binding: Mostly guidance or description ('needs', 'should', 'can help', 'possible measure'); EU043 says continuous compliance 'is required' within non-binding guidelines; EP2020 rationale text is descriptive.
themes.checks: Trigger: ongoing after deployment; regular or scheduled; on a performance drop or detected drift (retraining); when risks change. Compared against: expected operation; the identified risks; test data reflecting production data; the distribution of input data over time; the institution's own input data for bias. Metric or threshold: 'tracking performance', statistical accuracy where available, data drift measures; no thresholds. Who: not stated in most passages; controllers or EUIs. Result: retraining followed by validation of the new version; newly identified risks fed back into the risk process; correction of biased behaviour; otherwise not stated.

quotes.location: p.10, s.3.2 Lifecycle of an AI system (phase 6)
quotes.quote: Once deployed, the AI system is then operated by its users and needs continuous monitoring to ensure it operates as expected.
Retraining can be done on a fixed schedule (e.g. weekly or monthly) or triggered by performance drops or detected drift.
It is equally important to have control over the output data, including the inferences made by the model, which requires regular monitoring of that information, including human oversight.
the need for constant monitoring over time supported by continued feedback from user communities, be they citizens, businesses or public administration operators.
